item.title: Japan After the Landslide: Takaichi’s Supermajority and the Trump Challenge
item.description: Takaichi has the largest majority of any Japanese PM since World War II. Now she must decide how to tackle Japan’s difficult strategic environment.

item.title: Winds of Change: Can Taiwan’s Offshore Wind Deliver Fair Work Too?
item.description: Workers report debt-linked recruitment. Companies, financiers, and Taiwan’s government face a test of remedy.

item.title: Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami’s Election Doublespeak
item.description: The party’s constitution explicitly supports the implementation of Sharia. In their election speeches, leaders are singing a different tune.

item.title: The Geopolitics of India’s Foreign Assistance for 2026-27
item.description: In a region that increasingly benchmarks everything against China’s tempo, India’s aid will only buy influence when it also buys confidence.

item.title: Starlink Launches in Tajikistan
item.description: The satellite internet service's arrival offers hope for connectivity in mountainous regions, but pricing and state control remain concerns.

item.title: India-EU Trade is Set to Grow. Its Environmental Costs May Grow Faster.
item.description: The India-EU Free Trade Agreement is expected to expand exports and employment. But many of the sectors set to benefit are also among India’s most polluting.

item.title: What Will Happen to North Korean POWs in Ukraine?
item.description: The South Korean government has repeatedly conveyed its willingness to accept the soldiers as its citizens after the war.

item.title: Will Darwin Port Remain Under Chinese Control?
item.description: Australia’s prime minister pledged to reclaim operational control of the port. That still hasn’t happened, but the time might be drawing near.

item.description: China’s disinformation machinery kicked into high gear to launch its latest attack against the Tibetan spiritual leader.

item.title: Why Did Canadian Firm Laramide Abandon a Uranium Project in Kazakhstan?
item.description: Laramide President and CEO Marc Henderson called recent changes to the country's subsoil use law “a spectacular own goal." He characterized it as “de facto nationalization."
